title: HS2 and Euston: Reset, Reality, and the Road Ahead
label: 14 Sep 2026 · HS2 and Euston
summary: The Public Accounts Committee questioned Department for Transport and HS2 Ltd leaders about the HS2 programme's £87.7–102.7 billion cost, delays to 2040–43, the Euston reset, contract renegotiations, and land disposal. Witnesses defended the reset as a more realistic approach, while members pressed on governance, benefits, cancellation costs, and community impacts.

speakers.label: Dean Creamer
speakers.name: Dean Creamer
speakers.role: Director General, Major Rail Projects, Department for Transport

chapters.title: Opening Statements and Defence Savings
chapters.takeaway: The session opened with introductions and a brief discussion on how the Department for Transport will find £700 million in savings for the defence investment plan.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome, everyone. Today we're looking at HS2 and Euston. Before we dive into HS2, Jo, can you tell us how the Department will deliver the £700 million in savings needed for the defence investment plan?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: We're managing a 1% capital reduction across the spending review, and we've also committed to reduce roads funding by £700 million. The consultation on changing the road investment strategy closes today, and ministers will decide on any variations later in the autumn.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What about the economic impact of cancelling or changing road schemes?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: Ministers protected road maintenance funding. The difficult choices were about enhancements. The analysis is in the consultation, and I can't add much beyond that.

chapters.title: HS2 Cost Estimates and the Reset
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses defended the new £87.7–102.7 billion cost range as a realistic reset, acknowledging past failures but arguing that the programme is now on a more stable footing.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Now to HS2. Your latest estimate is up to £100 billion. How can you assure us it won't rise again?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: The NAO's statement that HS2 'has not gone as planned' is an understatement. But we've tackled root causes. The NAO recognised our work to stabilise cost, schedule, and governance.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: When I arrived in December 2024, the programme was uncoordinated, we didn't know where we were, and no figures could be relied on. We did a five-step reset. We found three systemic problems: starting too early without design, contracts that transferred all risk to HS2, and poor management. Now we have a reference case that's forward-leaning but realistic.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: We're forming a new baseline, 8.0, to replace the discredited 7.1. We aim to have it by Christmas, or by April next year. Then we'll bind the supply chain into the plan, with 8.1, so there's a clear line of sight from this Committee to the frontline.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Can you clarify 'backing off the supply chain'?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: It means getting agreement from our seven key contracts—four civils, two stations, and rolling stock—on the schedule and sequence. We may not conclude all commercial deals, but everyone must agree the plan is viable.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How long will that take, and does the uncertainty threaten the spring timescale?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: I can't guarantee it because it involves counterparties and assurance. But we're on the right trajectory. Two contracts are already reset. We hope to align BBV and SCS in the next two or three months. The stations and rolling stock should be done by March.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: We need a plan B if deals aren't done. There will be uncertainty to the end, but we'll manage it.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: The ranges include no-deal scenarios. We're confident they cover all but extreme events.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: That's a very wide envelope.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: Yes, but it reflects past over-optimism. We're tasked with getting to the lower end. The wide bookends recognise the real uncertainty.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: The ranges don't cover black swan events like hyperinflation or war. But they're robust for most things.

chapters.title: Speed Reduction and Technical Derisking
chapters.takeaway: Reducing train speed to 300–320 kph and removing automatic train operation will cut technical risk and cost without major benefit loss, aligning HS2 with proven European high-speed technology.

turns.speaker: Ruth Cadbury
turns.text: You've agreed to reduce speeds to 300 kph. How confident are you that this reduces risk and cost, and is there a downside?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: The Secretary of State asked Mark to look at speed to take out technical risk. For London to Birmingham, it's a three-minute difference, but still a 30-minute saving over conventional. Mark can explain the risk reduction.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: We don't want to be on the bleeding edge. This spec delivers 10 trains an hour and future-proofs 16. Reducing speed to 300–320 kph means we use the same technology and testing as France, Japan, Spain, and Italy. It converges with HS1 and derisks testing. Only China runs at 350 kph frequently, and they struggle to go beyond.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: We're also removing automatic train operation. That technology doesn't exist at the quality standard we need for high-speed. Taking it out means manual driving like HS1 or France. It removes huge testing effort. These changes derisk the project and help us aim for the earlier end of the ranges.

turns.speaker: Ruth Cadbury
turns.text: Is there a loss of benefit for future passengers?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: The railway will meet the 10 trains an hour specification reliably. Future governments could modify for 16 trains an hour if they build more lines. Spending £2–3 billion and two years to future-proof now isn't worthwhile because technology may change anyway. This aligns us with the best European railways and Network Rail's digital signalling.

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: We're avoiding a situation where a decade from now we'd have to explain why we spent billions but couldn't commission 360 kph.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: We were authorised to try for two years then revert. Lessons from other projects say deal with complexity early. The benefit-cost ratio doesn't change much. It's about derisking and allowing ministers to decide.

chapters.title: Benefits and Capacity
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses argued HS2's main benefit is capacity relief on the West Coast Main Line, not just speed, but members questioned demand assumptions and the logic of a slower line.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: I'm relatively new, but I've followed HS2. You've done a good job on Crossrail, Mark, but we've spent up to £102 billion for a line to Birmingham that won't be complete until 2043. Technology like AI may reduce travel demand. What are the benefits for the taxpayer?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: This is about capacity and connectivity on the West Coast Main Line. It's one of our most constrained corridors. HS2 will free up capacity for commuter services and improve reliability. Avanti's on-time performance was 57% in 2025-26. HS2 will more than double peak long-distance capacity from London to Birmingham.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: There'll be a 30-minute difference for London to Birmingham, 20 minutes quicker for other destinations, and 45% additional capacity. Plus regeneration: 49,000 jobs and 60,000 homes along the line.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: What modelling have you done on demand? With AI and remote work, how do you know there'll be demand?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: Demand has largely recovered since Covid. We expect 1–2% growth per year. The BCR assumes £36 billion in benefits, but if demand is higher, benefits increase. We've taken a cautious approach and will publish sensitivity analysis next year.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: I struggle to see the benefits of a slower line to Birmingham. Freight is mostly road-based, and making rail freight work would require more spending.

turns.speaker: Ruth Cadbury
turns.text: There's very little capacity for more passenger trains on West Coast, and freight companies are desperate for paths. How much freight capacity will HS2 free up?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: There's no number yet. Freight won't go on HS2. That balance will be for Great British Railways to decide through consultation.

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: The duties on Great British Railways include supporting the rail freight market, which is part of the legislation in the Lords.

chapters.title: Contracts, Cancellation Costs, and Commercial Tension
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses acknowledged that original contracts were flawed and difficult to renegotiate, but said new deals with EKFB and Align introduce cost control and delivery incentives; cancellation cost estimates were defended as conservative.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: As a contractor, am I right that the NEC3 cost-plus contracts were signed because the Government didn't know what it wanted, letting contractors benefit? And now they're hard to renegotiate?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: That's fair. Starting with immature design and asking the supply chain to fix a price was a root cause. At notice to proceed, there wasn't enough certainty for contractors to take risk, so it flowed back to HS2. The new risk process captures that. For the two civils we've reset, we've settled the past, fixed the fee to create tension, and added incentives for early delivery. We aim to do the same with SCS and BBV.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: But once you sign a duff contract, you're a hostage to the contractor. The NAO mentions potential £2 billion savings. Are you sure you'll make them?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: These contracts aren't a panacea, but they reintroduce tension. The £2 billion is about avoiding future risk. The contractors want to work for UK plc and move on. The EKFB reset cut exclusions from several hundred to fewer than 20. They've moved 15 million cubic metres of earth this year against a target of 16 million. The reset is working, but it's not perfect.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: We need the contractors to care about our money and to get off the job quickly. The firms that have signed deals are performing better.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: On cancellation costs, it looks like DFT and HS2 costed completion independently but not cancellation. Should that be independently verified?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: We asked Mark to assess remediation versus cancellation proportionately. We wanted him focused on executing the programme, not distracted. Mark can explain the methodology.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: The request was to verify methodology and range. We applied 35–55% of spent cost to complete, which felt prudent, plus 66% optimism bias per the Green Book. The law says I should replace every blade of grass, so it's conservative.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: The Green Book says 6–66%. You took the maximum. It looks like you're making facts fit the story to avoid embarrassment.

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: 66% is the appropriate optimism bias for a programme of this immaturity. Given how costs have inflated historically, it's prudent.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: Our contractual position isn't strong, and there's no organisation to handle claims from demobilising 30,000 people. The methodology is appropriate, perhaps conservative.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: In 2023, cancellation was £11 billion; now it's £33–58 billion. I'd have cancelled. Why go ahead before renegotiating contracts? The nuclear option strengthens your hand.

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: The decision to continue was made by the Government in 2023.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: HS2 underestimated costs then, so I wouldn't rely on that £11 billion. We've spent £25 billion since. With 34,000 people and £25 million spent daily, the supply chain wouldn't see cancellation as credible. Resetting contracts is the right way. We have good deals with EKFB and Align and aim for SCS and BBV.

chapters.title: Governance and Organisational Capability
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses described new governance structures and a strengthened HS2 organisation, but acknowledged the need to maintain capability and avoid ineffective bureaucracy.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: The NAO says HS2 is now a mega-project with new assurance processes. Has that changed your governance approach?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: Yes. We've removed duplicative layers and introduced integrated assurance. The new mega-project decision panel and ministerial taskforce have met seven times. I chair a new shareholder board with independent members. We're not complacent, but governance has improved.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: How do you avoid replacing one ineffective system with another?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: We keep it under review and learn lessons. We're reviewing the shareholder board. The proof is in the progress through reset. We'll continue to refine governance for each stage.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: We have a ministerial taskforce for strategic decisions, a shareholder board to keep us honest, and a performance board where Mark and I review progress monthly. Our teams meet weekly to work through issues. We can escalate as needed.

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: The relationship between the Department and HS2 is now much stronger, as the NAO observed.

turns.speaker: Ruth Cadbury
turns.text: Jo, what's the difference between a mega-project and critical national growth infrastructure?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: I may need to write on that.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: Mega-projects get bespoke governance, a full funding envelope, flexibilities for capability, and regular reporting. The threshold is about £10 billion, and NISTA decides designations. Critical national growth infrastructure can be private and is a planning definition.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: Mark, how will you address capability gaps?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: We've strengthened the board and executive team, added a chief commercial officer and chief programme director, and moved 300 roles from the corporate centre to the frontline. We're creating metrics for organisational health. We can't exit reset until we demonstrate the capability to deliver the baseline.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: Can you recruit and retain the staff you need?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: Yes. We'll always have a flex between permanent and contract staff, but we have no constraints on recruiting the right people. We're attracting good senior talent.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: Why wasn't the Crossrail approach used before?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: Some lessons were already applied. The key is transparency and one source of truth. Crossrail's integrated baseline had everything needed. We're ensuring fidelity in our new baseline. It's a balance, but we work on it daily.

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: We'll report transparently through the six-monthly parliamentary report, due before the end of the year.

chapters.title: Euston: Costs, Delivery Model, and Integration
chapters.takeaway: Euston cost estimates are less mature, and a new delivery company will act as a guiding mind, but funding depends on a robust plan and private sector engagement.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: The NAO says Euston could cost around £8 billion. Is that a mature estimate?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: Euston cost estimates are less mature. We now have an agreed spatial plan and the Euston Delivery Company as a single guiding mind. We won't refine numbers until we have a detailed concept design. This programme has failed twice; we can't let that happen again.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: James Stewart said get a delivery model and bring partners into the tent. The EDC board includes TfL, Network Rail, and HS2. We're appointing a chief executive now. Above that is a strategic board with ministers, the GLA, and Camden. Beneath is a delivery alliance for integration. Funding follows the plan.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: What's the EDC headcount, and when will it be fully operational?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: About 30 posts now, established as a business unit. It'll become an arms-length body in autumn. The CEO will assess capability needs. We can second experts from TfL and Network Rail.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: Will the new CEO and chair have a clear timeframe to develop a plan?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: Yes, but we won't set arbitrary dates. We want them to test the timeframe and give honest views. The next few years are planning. We need robust cost and schedule expectations before delivery.

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: We're also focused on improving the current station experience for passengers now.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: The redevelopment of Euston conventional station is listed as a major project. Is it a mega-project?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: It's not designated separately; it's part of the HS2 mega-project. It benefits from the same flexibilities. We'll discuss with NISTA and Treasury if separate designation becomes useful.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: It must not create competitive incentives with HS2. It's core to delivering Mark's ranges. We need the flexibilities without making it entirely separate.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: Are you learning from other projects on private finance?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: Yes. We have external expertise, work with Treasury and NISTA, and had 70 market responses. Concerns include inflation and interface management. We'll only do a deal if it's right for the taxpayer.

chapters.title: Passenger Experience and Community Impact
chapters.takeaway: Members pressed on integrating transport modes at Euston and mitigating disruption to local communities, with witnesses citing new co-ordination bodies and community funds.

turns.speaker: Ruth Cadbury
turns.text: Who is ensuring all transport choices—tube, rail, buses, bikes, taxis—are integrated into Euston's design from the start?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: The EDC brings all dutyholders together. TfL has flagged taxi and bus interchange and issues like tapping in and out at Euston Square. We'll sign off concept design only when all partners' requirements are met. Ambition versus affordability will be managed.

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: Andy Lord, the TfL commissioner, is personally engaged because Euston is central to London's transport system.

turns.speaker: Ruth Cadbury
turns.text: What about links to St Pancras for HS1?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: That's part of the flows work Dean described.

turns.speaker: Ruth Cadbury
turns.text: What steps are you taking to reduce impact on residents and businesses around Euston?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: The EDC will co-ordinate community engagement. HS2 has provided £2 million for mitigation, Camden £3.5 million. We've moved spoil by rail instead of road and will maintain community funds as long as needed.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: Drummond Street is one of the most disrupted communities. We've worked hard to help—the Euston hub and skills centre are successes. Moving spoil by rail takes 50 lorries off the road daily. But we need to stay focused on their needs. It's top of our agenda.

chapters.title: Land and Property Disposal
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses outlined a forthcoming strategy for disposing of surplus land and properties, acknowledging delays but committing to a balanced approach that protects taxpayers and local markets.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: You've bought vast amounts of land and property. Why has it taken so long to return surplus land, and what's your strategy?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: We have four property areas. The east Leeds leg has about 500 properties no longer needed; 300 have Crichel Down rules. An agent will provide a disposal strategy in autumn. We'll pilot soon and hope to have properties on the market this year. We must avoid flooding local markets and protect taxpayers.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Why the delay? Is it just bureaucracy?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: The picture is complicated by successive decisions—scaling back to phase 1 and the new commitment to build north from Birmingham to Manchester. We needed a strategy that supports communities and secures value.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: We have a moral obligation to sort this out quickly.

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: Absolutely.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: What about land you're retaining? You can't leave it unmanaged—it creates weed banks and costs money.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: We'll maintain properties, including listed ones. We rent out about 60% at market rates. Where possible, previous owners farm the land under lease. We have KPIs with HS2 on management and disposal, and ministers check regularly.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: When will you start returning unwanted land?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: Temporary land on phase 2a is starting now—filling 450 boreholes, completed in 18 months. Permanent land requires decisions.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: So it's in hand and not delayed?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: Yes, temporary land is under way.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Jo, will you commit to an independent review of cancellation costs?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: We made a proportionate assessment to keep Mark's team focused on delivery. We'll consider any Committee recommendation with ministers.

chapters.title: Closing: Mega-Project Designation and Final Thoughts
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses said they would keep Euston's mega-project designation under review and advocate for the best delivery conditions, as the session concluded.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: The NAO says Euston fits most characteristics of a mega-project. Will the Government designate it as one?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: It's not in my gift. We'll keep it under review with Treasury and NISTA and advocate for whatever gives Euston and HS2 the best conditions for success.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: At the moment, Euston doesn't lack any flexibilities it would get as a mega-project.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. That brings our session to an end. We appreciate your candour on a project with a troubled history. It's been useful to hear your update.
